## Port Lockroy: a museum stop on an Antarctic cruise

[Port Lockroy](/antarctica/place/port-lockroy/) is a sheltered bay off the western coast of Wiencke Island. The small Goudier Island is home to the buildings of historic British Base A, a museum, a post office, and a colony of gentoo penguins. Unlike most nature-focused stops on the Antarctic Peninsula, its main attraction is also connected with the history of exploration.

A visit to Port Lockroy is **possible**, but not guaranteed, on two of our sea expeditions. Whether the vessel can approach and passengers can land depends on sea conditions, the overall sailing schedule, and arrangements with the base staff.

## Which tours might include Port Lockroy?

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} in which this historic stop is listed as an additional possibility.

[Antarctica: Discovery and Learning Journey](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) lasts 11 days and 10 nights. The vessel departs from Ushuaia, crosses the Drake Passage, and spends several days around the Antarctic Peninsula. Port Lockroy, Jougla Point, and natural bays are among the possible locations during days 4–7. Wildlife watching, marine scenery, and the history of Antarctic exploration are central to the journey.

[Antarctica: Discovery and Long Hikes](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/) has a similar duration and geographic coverage but additionally offers **possible hiking activities**. In suitable conditions, these may include snowshoeing near [Damoy Point](/antarctica/place/damoy-point/) and a hike on Deception Island. These activities require separate assessment of conditions, physical demands, and equipment. Visiting the Port Lockroy museum remains an ordinary historic stop, subject to permission.

Both itineraries cross the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/) and end in [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). There is therefore no need to choose the second trip just for the museum: the possible stop appears in both programs.

## Historic Base A and life among polar explorers

Port Lockroy Base was established in 1944 as part of the British Operation Tabarin. Polar personnel lived and worked here until the station closed in 1962. The surviving buildings were later restored and turned into a heritage site.

Bransfield House contains a museum, shop, and post office. The exhibition tells the story of scientific work and daily life for a small team in Antarctica. Today, the site is cared for by the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust, and the nearby gentoo penguin colony is monitored.

This experience is quite different from a landing made to see glaciers or landscapes. Visitors can discover the **human-made heritage of polar expeditions**, before returning to a region of immense ice slopes and mountains.

Nearby [Jougla Point](/antarctica/place/jougla-point/) is also listed among possible locations on both itineraries. But the proximity of the two shores does not mean the vessel will necessarily visit them both.

## Why the museum and post office cannot be promised in advance

Goudier Island is an active seasonal heritage site. The official visitor guidelines explicitly state that visits to the base must be arranged with its manager. Some paths are restricted to protect penguins, while visitor numbers and building access are regulated.

During the 2026/27 season, the UK Antarctic Heritage Trust is continuing major conservation work on the historic structures. This does not in itself mean the whole complex is closed, but it explains why actual visiting conditions, timing, and access to buildings need confirmation.

Even if the base is open, landings by boat depend on sea conditions. If going ashore is impossible, the expedition may continue toward other coastal locations. **A Port Lockroy postmark is also not guaranteed**: using the post office requires an actual visit and the service to be available on that day.

## How to choose between the two expeditions

If the main attraction is the historic base and the overall Antarctic experience, compare the dates, cabin category, and complete list of possible stops. If you want to combine the sea cruise with longer hikes ashore, consider the hiking itinerary as well. The presence of such an option in a description does not guarantee that it will take place or automatically establish how physically demanding it will be.

In both cases, a Port Lockroy visit should be viewed as **a meaningful addition** to a cruise around [Antarctica](/antarctica/), not a service on a guaranteed date. The current programs do not specify a separate museum-visit price or promise an admission ticket.

We can help compare the actual itineraries, duration of ocean crossings, and preferred activity formats. Related routes are available in the [Antarctic tours catalog](/antarctica/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about Port Lockroy

### Is the museum a mandatory part of the expedition?

No. Port Lockroy is listed as a possible stop. Landing depends on navigational conditions and permission from the base manager.

### Can you mail a postcard from the Antarctic post office?

This is possible when the post office is operating and you visit it, but a particular sailing does not guarantee a landing or access to the service.

### Is the museum visit different from a walk near Damoy Point?

Yes. Port Lockroy is a historic museum site. Snowshoeing near Damoy Point is a separate potential activity on the itinerary offering longer hikes.

### Do you need to set aside a full day for Port Lockroy?

The current itineraries do not have a fixed day dedicated to the museum. It is considered among possible stops during Antarctic days 4–7; the expedition team determines the sequence.

## Rongé Island: mountains and glaciers above the Errera Channel

**Rongé Island lies off the western coast of the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/), near the Errera Channel.** From the sea, its steep rocky slopes, snow, and glaciers descending toward the water make it easy to recognize.

The principal attraction here is the **marine scenery**. You do not have to land on the island to appreciate its geography: the contrast between dark rocks, snow, and a narrow waterway is clearly visible from a ship's deck or on an authorized expedition boat outing.

## Where is the island, and what makes the Errera Channel distinctive?

Rongé lies off Graham Land and forms the western side of the Errera Channel. To the east are the Antarctic Peninsula coastline and neighboring islands. This is a region of steep mountains, narrow waterways, and glacial slopes.

In the international Antarctic geographic gazetteer, Rongé is described as **a high, rocky island approximately 8 km long**. On Antarctic maps, it belongs to a group of islands near the western side of the Errera Channel.

What distinguishes such channels is the proximity of mountain slopes to the water. During an open-ocean crossing, the surrounding landscape feels different: coasts are far away or not visible at all. Near Rongé, the mountains enclose the waterway, turning even a relatively short passage into a memorable experience.

[Cuverville Island](/antarctica/place/cuverville-island/) is also associated with this area, set among the mountains of the peninsula and Rongé Island. On an [Antarctic journey](/antarctica/), Cuverville can be considered primarily a possible place to observe gentoo penguins, while Rongé showcases the rugged terrain of a mountainous island.

## Why is the island called Rongé?

The island was explored by members of the **Belgian Antarctic Expedition of 1897–1899**, led by Adrien de Gerlache. The expedition mapped numerous features on the western Antarctic Peninsula.

The name honors **Madame de Rongé**, who supported the expedition. This story survives in Antarctic geographic records and recalls a time when coastlines and islands were still being mapped from observations aboard ships.

Modern maps use the spelling **Rongé Island**, while forms in other languages vary. All refer to the same island, not to several separate places on an itinerary.

## What can you see around Rongé Island?

The main impression is the combination of high snow-covered mountains, precipitous shores, and sea ice. In clear weather, the lines of glaciers and rocks are visible, while clouds sometimes hide the island's upper slopes. Low-angle light helps reveal the terrain particularly well.

| From the sea | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Mountain slopes | Boundaries between snow and rock |
| Glaciers | Shapes of icy slopes |
| Errera Channel | Proximity of islands and coast |
| Sea ice | Movement of ice floes on the water |

Wildlife may be seen in Antarctic waters, but **particular species and encounters at Rongé Island are not guaranteed**. If penguins are the focus of your journey, consider nearby areas, including [Cuverville](/antarctica/place/cuverville-island/), where colonies are mentioned in the itineraries.

## How does the island feature in Ada Tours expeditions?

In the [Antarctica: Beyond the Antarctic Circle expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/), Rongé Island is part of the wider geography of possible visits in the peninsula region. However, the Antarctic Peninsula itself forms part of the main day-by-day itinerary, while the expedition team chooses the precise islands and bays according to ice conditions.

This distinction matters. The journey may introduce travelers to the straits and islands off the western coast, but **passing directly by Rongé or landing on its shore cannot be considered a guaranteed part of the trip**.

When choosing an expedition, compare more than a list of place names: consider how long the vessel spends in Antarctic waters, its intended direction, opportunities for Zodiac excursions, and how the route may change in poor weather. You can explore the general format in the [cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/) section.

## Weather and restrictions on approaches by sea

In Antarctica, sea ice, wind, waves, and visibility can change the captain's and expedition leader's decisions even during a single day. Navigating a narrow channel requires careful assessment. In dense ice or difficult weather, the team may choose a different bay or observe from the ship instead.

For travelers, **the geographic list describes route possibilities**, not a schedule of mandatory landings. Bring windproof clothing, a waterproof outer layer, and protection for your camera. Wind makes it feel colder on an open deck.

During shore landings and boat outings, IAATO conservation rules apply: wildlife must not be disturbed, the team's instructions must be followed, and site-specific restrictions must be respected.

## Frequently asked questions about Rongé Island

### Where is Rongé Island?

Off the western coast of the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/), on the western side of the Errera Channel.

### Where does the name Rongé come from?

The island was named after Madame de Rongé, who supported the Belgian Antarctic Expedition in the late 19th century.

### Can you see the island without landing?

Yes. Its high slopes and glaciers are clearly visible from the sea when the ship's route and visibility permit.

### Is Rongé Island included in every cruise?

No. In the [Ada Tours expedition itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/), it is one of the possible locations during the Antarctic stage. The actual passage depends on ice and weather.

## Rongé Island: what an optional expedition location means

[Rongé Island](/antarctica/place/ronge-island/) lies off the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula. Its mountainous slopes and glaciers form the western side of the Errera Channel. For travelers aboard an expedition ship, its main attractions are dramatic snowy panoramas, a narrow sea passage, and proximity to natural areas where birds can be observed.

On our current itinerary, Rongé is listed as **a possible route location**, but a separate shore landing is not guaranteed. The tour mentions the island in its description of nearby Cuverville. Seeing Rongé from the water and landing at its northern tip are different scenarios.

## What is found around Rongé?

The island extends along the Errera Channel, with [Cuverville Island](/antarctica/place/cuverville-island/) nearby. Mountainous islands, rocky shores, and glaciers alternate throughout the surrounding area. On a sea passage, travelers can observe the coastal landscape from the deck, but the ship's position and visibility depend on actual weather conditions.

Our itinerary mentions gentoo penguins and brown skuas at Cuverville. Those are **features of a separate location**: Cuverville's colonies must not automatically be presented as promised sightings on Rongé. The possibility of seeing wildlife depends on nature, season, and access to the area.

At the northern tip of Rongé is Georges Point. Official Antarctic visitor guidelines have been published for this site. They describe a rocky shore, colonies of gentoo and chinstrap penguins, and a guided route to a viewpoint. However, the existence of an authorized visitor area does not mean every ship in the Errera Channel makes a landing here.

## Which tour includes Rongé Island?

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} with a potential visit to the Rongé area.

[Antarctica: Beyond the Antarctic Circle](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-polar-circle-deep-south-13-days/) is a 13-day expedition from [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/) via the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/). Days 4–10 are dedicated to the Antarctic Peninsula, possible shore landings, and the journey south. Possible areas include Cuverville, Neko Harbour, and Paradise Bay, with Pléneau and Petermann Islands farther south.

Rongé appears in the description of this stage as a geographic reference point near Cuverville. However, the itinerary does not contain a separate **"Rongé day"** or a mandatory landing at Georges Point.

The expedition lasts **13 days and 12 nights**, starting on 6 March 2027. The objective of its southern stage is an attempt to cross the Antarctic Circle, ice permitting. The specific shore activities during days 4–10 are determined by the weather, ice, sea conditions, and the expedition team's decisions.

## Can you land at Georges Point?

Georges Point does have an official visitor site. Guidelines issued by the Antarctic Treaty Secretariat provide for a landing place, escorted walking route, and closed areas near nesting birds.

They warn of slippery rocks and dangerous terrain above the permitted area. Visitors must follow the designated route, give animals the right of way, and maintain sufficient distance. Scientific equipment is also present on shore and must not be approached without permission.

**These guidelines are not the same as the itinerary of a particular cruise.** Even if a vessel passes close by, an actual shore visit requires suitable conditions, an agreed plan, and permission from the expedition team. Our current tour does not include a mandatory visit to Rongé.

## How to choose an Antarctic itinerary

If your main interest is seascapes and mountainous islands, the Rongé area fits naturally into a journey around the western peninsula. It can be appreciated as part of a wider voyage even when the expedition remains on the water.

If **penguin colonies** are more important, compare the actual selection of possible stops around [Cuverville](/antarctica/place/cuverville-island/) and elsewhere on the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/). If you would prefer more walking, explore [adventure expeditions](/interests/adventure/tours/) and their confirmed hiking sections. A thematic label alone does not establish the duration or difficulty of any particular walk.

We can help compare current [Antarctic tours](/antarctica/tour/) by geography, number of days, and the format of possible landings. If reaching Rongé specifically is essential, discuss that in advance: the current itinerary does not guarantee such a visit.

## Frequently asked questions about Rongé Island

### Is a landing on Rongé guaranteed?

No. The island is listed in the general geography of the current 13-day tour, but no separate mandatory landing is specified.

### What is Georges Point?

It is a coastal visitor site at the northern end of Rongé, with rules protecting birds and governing safe visitor movement.

### Can you see Rongé while visiting Cuverville?

Both islands lie in the Errera Channel area. The vessel's actual course and visibility depend on navigation and weather.

### Does "Can be added" mean a paid excursion to the island?

No. The section indicates a potential geographic connection with a current tour. The itinerary does not specify a fixed price or guarantee a landing on Rongé.

## Schollaert Channel: a sea passage between Brabant and Anvers Islands

**The Schollaert Channel** is in the Palmer Archipelago, off the western [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/). It runs between the large islands of [Brabant](/antarctica/place/brabant-island/) and [Anvers](/antarctica/place/anvers-island/), connecting Dallmann Bay to the [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/).

For passengers aboard an expedition vessel, this is a sea passage between glaciated shores and snow-covered mountains. The channel itself is not a separate island, beach, or mandatory landing site. Its appeal lies in the geography of the passage: varied island landscapes appear close together, while the actual route depends on ice and weather.

## Where the channel runs on the map

According to the international SCAR Antarctic gazetteer, the Schollaert Channel runs northwest to southeast between the Joubin Peninsula on Brabant Island and coastal sections of Anvers Island. It links the waters of Dallmann Bay with those of the Gerlache Strait.

This is a useful reference point for understanding Antarctic maps. To the northwest lie the [Melchior Islands](/antarctica/place/melchior-islands/) in Dallmann Bay. To the southeast are other waterways where expeditions may observe glaciers and island coasts.

### Why the channel's name matters on an itinerary

On a cruise itinerary, Schollaert Channel identifies a particular geographic passage. If the Melchior Islands, Brabant, and Gerlache are also listed, these places are geographically connected, but should not be treated as one and the same stop.

Passing through the channel depends on the captain's decisions. Water appearing on a chart does not mean there will be a safe navigable route between icebergs on a particular day.

## What can be seen from aboard?

### Glacial slopes and islands

On both sides are stretches of land with mountain ridges, snowy slopes, and glaciers. In good visibility, travelers can distinguish the shape of the island shores and see where ice and rock meet the water. Brabant has particularly pronounced mountainous terrain.

The colors of water, ice, and rock change with the weather. Low cloud can conceal the summits even if the passage itself remains visible. This is one reason an expedition itinerary cannot be reduced to a list of guaranteed photographs.

### Icebergs and navigation at sea

Floating ice can accumulate near certain shores and along the direction of currents. The captain chooses the vessel's course with regard to the size of ice floes, wind, and sea conditions. Watching the navigation from an open deck can be interesting, but ship safety rules must be followed in strong winds.

Unlike the long ocean crossing through the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/), Schollaert is an internal sea channel of the archipelago, where land is constantly visible around the vessel.

## Where did the name Schollaert come from?

According to the SCAR Gazetteer, the channel was mapped during the Belgian Antarctic Expedition in 1898. It is named after François Schollaert, a Belgian statesman who supported the expedition. Names like this recall the first systematic explorations of island Antarctica.

For modern itineraries, it is useful to know the English form **Schollaert Channel**. It helps identify the same feature on maps and explains why its Russian rendering can have several spellings.

## Can you see the channel on a cruise?

Yes. The channel appears on expedition itineraries in the peninsula region. On the [11-day Discovery itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/), Schollaert is associated with the surrounding islands. It is also part of the confirmed route geography of the [whale-watching expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-whale-watching-learning-11-days/).

The two journeys cover some of the same natural areas but have different emphases. When choosing, compare the planned time in Antarctic waters, educational activities, and the type of excursions available from the particular ship.

A ship may pass through the channel without stopping. A route near Brabant and Anvers does not imply a landing on each island.

## How Schollaert differs from nearby geographic names

| Name | Type of feature |
| --- | --- |
| Schollaert | Sea channel |
| Brabant | Large island |
| Melchior | Group of small islands |

The [Melchior Islands](/antarctica/place/melchior-islands/) may appear near Dallmann Bay before or after passage through Schollaert. The [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/) belongs to the wider expedition geography but is a separate body of water.

Each has its own role: islands offer coastal landscapes, while channels provide routes between them.

## Weather, season, and safety

Expedition cruises in the Palmer Archipelago generally take place during the Antarctic summer. Weather remains unpredictable even then, and ice conditions can change rapidly. The ship's team decides whether to navigate the passage.

Warm layers and wind protection are needed for observing from the deck. Small-boat outings, if organized in a nearby bay, require a separate briefing and permission. Antarctic environmental rules prohibit disturbing wildlife or entering closed stretches of shore.

## Frequently asked questions about the Schollaert Channel

### Where is the Schollaert Channel?

Between Brabant and Anvers Islands in the Palmer Archipelago, off the western Antarctic Peninsula.

### Which waterways does it connect?

Dallmann Bay and the Gerlache Strait.

### Can an expedition ship's passage be guaranteed?

No. The vessel may change course according to ice, wind, and other navigational conditions.

### Why are there different spellings of the name?

The Russian form "Shollart" renders a French-Belgian surname; the international geographic name is Schollaert Channel.

## Which tours travel through the Schollaert Channel?

[Schollaert Channel](/antarctica/place/schollaert-channel/) lies in the Palmer Archipelago off the western coast of Antarctica. On one side is [Anvers Island](/antarctica/place/anvers-island/); on the other is [Brabant](/antarctica/place/brabant-island/). From a ship, travelers can enjoy views of their high snow-covered shores, glaciers, rocky areas, and waters dotted with floating ice.

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that feature Schollaert on their main route. All the current itineraries here last 11 days and 10 nights and begin in [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/). After sailing along the Beagle Channel and crossing the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/), the ship reaches Antarctic waters and explores the islands and peninsula coast.

| Traveler's interest | Itinerary |
|---|---|
| Polar nature | [Discovery and Learning](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) |
| Marine mammals | [Whale Watching](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-whale-watching-learning-11-days/) |
| Active pursuits | [Long Hikes](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/) |

The three itineraries cover similar waters around Anvers and Brabant but differ in what draws travelers to the expedition. To choose, compare the activities rather than looking only for differences in the channel name.

## Where Schollaert runs and what it is often confused with

Schollaert runs northwest to southeast from Dallmann Bay to the [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/). The official SCAR Antarctic geographic gazetteer describes it as a passage between the Joubin Peninsula on Brabant Island and island areas near Anvers. This is an important geographic detail: Schollaert connects two bodies of water; it is not a separate island or bay.

Nearby are the [Melchior Islands](/antarctica/place/melchior-islands/), a small group of islets in Dallmann Bay. Melchior and Schollaert may be mentioned together in route descriptions, but they refer to different features. Melchior is an island group, while Schollaert is a passage between two larger islands. Sailing near one does not prove that the ship entered the other.

The channel's name is linked to the Belgian Antarctic Expedition in the late 19th century. Its southeastern entrance was mapped in 1898, and it was named for the Belgian statesman Frans Schollaert, who supported the expedition. These details connect the scenery with the history of exploration in western Antarctica.

## Why the area is interesting on a sea expedition

Much of the experience here happens while sailing. If the vessel passes through the channel in good visibility, travelers can see opposing island shores, glacial slopes, and mountain ridgelines. The width of the passage and changing light reveal the varied terrain of this part of the Palmer Archipelago.

However, **navigating the channel remains a decision made at sea**. Wind, ice density, and the ability to maneuver safely all affect the route. Even when Schollaert is listed in the intended itinerary, the ship's actual track may change. A particular panorama from one side of the deck, an exact entrance time, or a landing on its shores cannot be promised beforehand.

The area is best understood alongside the [Melchior Islands](/antarctica/place/melchior-islands/) and [Anvers Island](/antarctica/place/anvers-island/). Together, they explain the geography of one section of the voyage. But activities on an individual sailing may take place elsewhere along the [Antarctic Peninsula](/antarctica/place/antarctic-peninsula/) if those sites are accessible in the weather.

## Three itineraries: similar routes, different activities

### An expedition to discover Antarctica

The [Discovery and Learning journey](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) plans an Antarctic section through the Melchior Islands and Schollaert Channel area. The itinerary centers on discovering Antarctic scenery and nature. The wider list of possible sites also includes Danco Island, Neko Harbour, Paradise Bay, and Port Lockroy.

These places belong to the geographic scope of the expedition; the schedule of visits can change. Choose this option for its expedition content and an interest in the polar environment, rather than for a promise to explore every named island.

### An expedition focused on whale watching

The [11-day whale-watching journey](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-whale-watching-learning-11-days/) includes Schollaert and nearby islands. Its distinctive theme is marine wildlife. Observations may take place from the vessel at different stages of the route as animals move and conditions change.

**Schollaert Channel itself cannot be treated as a guaranteed place to see whales.** More useful considerations for choosing this program include the time spent in Antarctic waters, viewing conditions, and expedition activities. You can compare options in the [Antarctic nature tours catalog](/interests/wildlife/tours/antarctica/).

### An expedition with longer hikes

On the [Discovery and Long Hikes itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/), the sea journey near Anvers and Schollaert is complemented by opportunities for activities elsewhere on the route. Possible options include hikes and outings in areas suitable for these activities.

It is important to distinguish **activity across the expedition as a whole** from landing specifically on Schollaert's shores. This program does not promise a hike along the channel itself. The conditions for shore excursions and the preparation required depend on the particular activity.

## Schollaert: a landing site or a stretch of sea passage?

The channel is usually mentioned as part of the sea route. When choosing a tour, distinguish between passage by ship, an outing in a Zodiac boat, and landing ashore. Travelers may see Schollaert's shores from the deck while all planned land activities take place at other accessible sites.

A landing requires a suitable place on the coast. The expedition team assesses sea conditions, moving ice, environmental requirements, and the ability to use boats safely. A shore being accessible on an earlier sailing does not guarantee access on another date.

Under IAATO guidelines, Antarctic visitors must not approach wildlife in ways that alter animal behavior and must comply with biosecurity requirements. Even if penguins, seals, or whales appear near the ship, observation must respect wildlife protection rules.

## How to choose a journey through Schollaert

The starting logistics for all three current 11-day journeys are similar: Ushuaia, the Beagle Channel, the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/), Antarctic waters, and the return crossing. As the overall duration is the same, comparing just the number of days reveals little.

Instead, think about what draws you to Antarctica:

- To discover the landscapes and expedition wildlife, consider the [Discovery and Learning program](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/).
- For a focus on marine animals, explore the [Whale-Watching expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-whale-watching-learning-11-days/).
- For additional active outings, compare the [Long Hikes itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/).

For each program, check the stated activities, participant requirements, accommodation, included services, and procedures for possible changes. The name "Schollaert" alone tells you little about these conditions.

## What to consider during the Antarctic sailing season

Expedition cruises around the Antarctic Peninsula take place in the Southern Hemisphere's summer season. Even then, strong winds, fog, cold, and drifting ice are possible. Weather changes between consecutive days may alter the order of sea passages.

Flying to Ushuaia is only the beginning of the journey. The sea expedition includes a Drake Passage crossing, where the ship may roll in the swell. Planning should take into account the itinerary's duration and your tolerance for ocean crossings. Warm clothing, waterproof protection, suitable footwear for shore outings, and following the accompanying team's instructions are especially important if you intend to join land-based activities.

For a broader view, explore [all Antarctic cruises and expeditions](/interests/cruises-and-expeditions/tours/antarctica/) and the [general Antarctic tours catalog](/antarctica/tour/). These sections help compare different durations and routes, but the presence of Schollaert on another cruise must always be confirmed against its own itinerary.

## Frequently asked questions about tours through the Schollaert Channel

### Where is the Schollaert Channel?

It lies between [Anvers](/antarctica/place/anvers-island/) and [Brabant](/antarctica/place/brabant-island/), connecting Dallmann Bay to the [Gerlache Strait](/antarctica/place/gerlache-strait/). It is a sea passage in the Palmer Archipelago.

### Do all Schollaert tours pass the Melchior Islands?

Both areas appear in the geography of the three current 11-day itineraries. However, the vessel's team determines the actual course and sequence of passages. Mentioning both names does not guarantee passage through every channel.

### Is a landing on the shore near Schollaert guaranteed?

No. [Schollaert](/antarctica/place/schollaert-channel/) is primarily an area for marine navigation. Landings are arranged at accessible permitted sites in suitable weather, which may require the itinerary to change.

### Can you see whales in this area?

Whale encounters are possible in western Antarctica, but the exact place and time are not known in advance. If this is your main priority, explore the [whale-watching expedition](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-whale-watching-learning-11-days/), keeping in mind that even a themed itinerary does not guarantee a sighting in Schollaert.

### Where does the journey begin?

All three featured itineraries start in [Ushuaia](/argentina/place/ushuaia/) and head toward the peninsula via the [Drake Passage](/antarctica/place/drake-passage/). Each lasts 11 days and 10 nights.

### How do you choose between an educational and an active expedition?

Compare the included activities. The [Discovery journey](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-learning-11-days/) emphasizes learning about nature, while the [Long Hikes itinerary](/antarctica/tour/antarctica-discovery-long-hikes-11-days/) adds a different kind of activity. Their sea routes around Schollaert are similar, so the deciding factors are the activities and participant requirements.
